792.title: The Ansar weep
792.hook: after Hunayn the Ansar feel left out of the gifts, and he tells them: others go home with sheep and camels, and you with the messenger
792.howItsDone: Muslims retell the Prophet's speech to the Ansar after Hunayn from Sahih al-Bukhari and the sirah, and his words about the valley of the Ansar are quoted when people speak of the bond between him and the people of Medina.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the forgiven: Wahshi, Hind and Ikrimah came, and were received. Your line was: the door stayed open.

After the battle of Hunayn, there's a great deal to hand out. And the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, gives generously, to leaders from Mecca and the tribes who have only just come over to Islam. The Ansar, the people of Medina who took him in when he had to leave Mecca, receive nothing from it. They notice. Some of the younger men talk. He gives to Quraysh, they say, while our swords still drip with their blood. Word reaches him. Today: the Ansar weep.
screen: `THE GIFTS OF HUNAYN.` → `NOTHING FOR THE ANSAR.` → `SOME OF THE YOUNG MEN TALK.`

segments.voice: In Sahih al-Bukhari, he doesn't send a message. He gathers the Ansar in one place, just them, and speaks to them directly. First he reminds them of what they've been through together. Didn't I find you astray, and Allah guided you through me? Divided, and Allah brought you together? In need, and Allah made you rich? To each line they answer: Allah and His messenger are more generous. Then he turns it around. In Bukhari he tells them that if they wished, they could answer him back: you came to us like this, and like this. Ibn Ishaq's sirah fills it in: you came to us rejected, and we believed you; alone, and we helped you. He says their side of the story out loud for them. Won't you be content, he asks, that people go home with sheep and camels, and you go home with the messenger of Allah? If people took one valley and the Ansar another, he would take the valley of the Ansar. In Ibn Ishaq's sirah, this is where they weep, until their beards are wet, and they say: we're content with the messenger of Allah as our share. One way to read it: the hurt wasn't really about camels. It was about whether they still mattered to him. So he didn't hand them more goods. He told them, plainly and in front of each other, what they meant to him. And after the conquest of Mecca, his own city, he went home to Medina with them, and stayed.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has stood by you without much thanks and might feel a little overlooked: a parent, a friend, a coworker who covers for you. The way he did, say their side for them, quietly: you were there when I needed you. Then find the one plain sentence you'd want them to hear, not a gift, a sentence; if you pray, you can ask Allah to bless them.
Ansar, 'the helpers,' the people of Medina who felt left out of the gifts after Hunayn, until the Prophet told them they would go home with him. Today's word.
Your line: you go home with me. Not sheep or camels: him. That's day seven hundred ninety-two.

793.title: The heat of Tabuk
793.hook: in the heat before Tabuk, Uthman equips the army, and Abu Dharr walks alone behind it
793.howItsDone: Muslims retell the campaign of Tabuk from the Qur'an's ninth surah, the hadith collections and the sirah, and Uthman's gift and Abu Dharr's walk are told as two pictures of giving in hardship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ansar wept, and heard: others take sheep and camels, you take the messenger home. Your line was: you go home with me.

Summer in Medina. Ka'b ibn Malik, in Sahih al-Bukhari, remembers the fruit ripe and the shade inviting. And the call goes out to march north toward Tabuk, a long way through hard heat. The Qur'an itself records what those who stayed behind said: don't go out in this heat. It answers them that the fire of hell is fiercer in heat, if only they understood. That's surah nine, al-Tawbah. The army that gathers has a name in the hadith: the army of hardship. Today: the heat of Tabuk.
screen: `SUMMER, AND RIPE FRUIT.` → `DON'T GO OUT IN THIS HEAT.` → `THE ARMY OF HARDSHIP.`

segments.voice: Two people stand out in this march. The first is Uthman ibn Affan. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, asks who will equip the army of hardship, Sahih al-Bukhari reports that Uthman did it. The collection of al-Tirmidhi adds a scene: Uthman pours coins into the Prophet's lap, and the Prophet turns them over in his hands and says that nothing Uthman does after this day will harm him. A generous man, giving from plenty, at the moment it counts. The second is Abu Dharr. The sirah of Ibn Ishaq tells that his camel is too slow and weak to keep up. He falls behind. So he takes his things off the camel, puts them on his own back, and walks, following the army's tracks through the heat. Later, in camp, someone sees a lone figure coming along the road. The Prophet says: let it be Abu Dharr. And it is. Then he says words about Abu Dharr that the sirah remembers: may Allah have mercy on him, he walks alone, he will die alone, and he will be raised alone. Put the two side by side. One gives a fortune. One gives his own two feet. Neither one waits for the conditions to be good. Uthman doesn't wait until giving is easy. Abu Dharr doesn't wait for a better camel. And the Prophet sees both of them, the man with the coins in his lap and the man too far back for anyone else to notice.
screen: `WHO WILL EQUIP THE ARMY?` · `UTHMAN GIVES FROM PLENTY.` · `ABU DHARR'S CAMEL GIVES OUT.` · `HE CARRIES HIS OWN LOAD.` · then, large: `ALONE, WALKING BEHIND.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one shared thing that needs help, a mosque, a food bank, a school fund, a neighbor's repair, and if a voice says later, when things are easier, notice it. Then ask which kind of giving fits you: Uthman's, from what you have, or Abu Dharr's, your own time and effort, carried on your back. If you pray, you can ask Allah to accept it.
Tabuk, the hard summer march where Uthman equipped the army of hardship and Abu Dharr, his camel failing, walked alone behind it. Today's word.
Your line: alone, walking behind. A fortune and two feet, both seen. Day seven hundred ninety-three.

794.title: The Christians of Najran
794.hook: a Christian delegation from Najran is received in the mosque in Medina, and prays there
794.howItsDone: Muslims retell the visit of the Najran delegation from the sirah and the hadith, and the scene of the Christians praying in the Prophet's mosque is cited in conversations about hospitality between Muslims and Christians.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heat of Tabuk: Uthman's gift, and Abu Dharr on foot. Your line was: alone, walking behind.

Visitors from Najran, far to the south, walk into the Prophet's mosque in Medina just after the afternoon prayer. They are Christians, scholars and leaders of their community, dressed in fine robes, and they have come to talk with the Prophet about who Jesus is. They have come a long way, with real questions, and they are guests. Then their own time of prayer comes, there in the mosque. What happens next is the story. Today: the Christians of Najran.
screen: `THE MOSQUE AT MEDINA.` → `VISITORS FROM NAJRAN.` → `THEIR TIME OF PRAYER COMES.`

segments.voice: The sirah of Ibn Ishaq tells it simply. The Christians of Najran stand up to pray, in their own way, inside the mosque. And the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells the people around him: let them be. So they pray in the mosque of Medina, facing east. Hold that picture. Guests of another faith, praying their own prayer, under the same roof, and the host telling everyone to leave them in peace. Then come the conversations, and they're real. The two sides disagree about Jesus, honestly and at length. Muslims honor Jesus as a prophet and the Messiah; the Christians of Najran believe him to be the Son of God. Tradition links verses of the Qur'an's third surah to this visit. Among them is an invitation the Qur'an addresses to the People of the Scripture: come to a word that is common between us and you, to worship none but God. The talks don't end with everyone agreeing. Sahih al-Bukhari records that the leaders of Najran made an agreement with the Prophet and went home, and they asked him to send a trustworthy man back with them. He chose Abu Ubaydah, and called him the trustworthy one of this community. So the story holds three things together. Real disagreement, stated plainly. Real hospitality, down to the place of prayer. And a relationship that continues, with a trusted person sent along.

795.title: The farewell sermon, in full
795.hook: at Arafah: your blood and property are sacred, treat women well, all of you are from Adam, and Adam from dust
795.howItsDone: Muslims read the farewell sermon from the hadith collections, where its parts are spread across several narrations, and it is recited and taught at the time of the hajj and in Friday sermons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Najran's Christians prayed in the mosque: let them be. Your line was: guests in the mosque.

The plain of Arafah, outside Mecca, on the day of the pilgrimage. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is on what Muslims call the farewell pilgrimage. Jabir ibn Abdullah, in Sahih Muslim, tells how he rides into the valley and speaks to the people. His first words tie three sacred things together: your blood and your property are sacred to you, as sacred as this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this city of yours. Today: the farewell sermon.
screen: `THE PLAIN OF ARAFAH.` → `HE SPEAKS TO THE PEOPLE.` → `AS SACRED AS THIS DAY.`

segments.voice: The sermon isn't one document; its lines are spread across the hadith collections, each narrator keeping a part. Jabir's account keeps his words about women: be mindful of God in how you treat them, for you have taken them on a trust from God. The next day, the day of sacrifice at Mina, Bukhari reports him asking: what day is this? What month? What city? In Abu Bakrah's report, each time the crowd answers: Allah and His messenger know best. Then: your blood, your property and your honor are as sacred to one another as this day, in this month, in this city. A sacred day, month and city, laid over every person in front of him. In reports in Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, which some readers gather into the sermon, he says people are all children of Adam, and Adam was made from dust. No Arab has any merit over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, no light-skinned person over a dark-skinned one, nor the reverse, except by mindfulness of God. The Qur'an says something close in surah forty-nine: humankind was made into nations and tribes so that they might know one another, and the noblest in God's sight is the most mindful of Him. In Jabir's account, he asks what they will say of him; they answer that he has conveyed the message. He raises his finger to the sky, points it toward the people, and says: O Allah, bear witness. And in Bukhari he tells those present to pass it on to those who are absent. That instruction is part of why you're hearing it now.
screen: `AS SACRED AS THIS DAY.` · `A TRUST FROM GOD.` · `CHILDREN OF ADAM, ADAM FROM DUST.` · `PASS IT TO THOSE ABSENT.` · then, large: `ALL FROM ADAM.`

Let each one sit for a few breaths, and if you pray, you can ask Allah to help you live by it.

796.title: The last days
796.hook: in his final illness he leaves no slave behind, gives away his last coins, and asks for the prayer to be kept
796.howItsDone: Muslims retell the Prophet's final illness from the hadith collections, and his last instruction about the prayer and those in one's care is quoted in teaching about salah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the farewell sermon at Arafah: blood and property sacred, women a trust, everyone from Adam. Your line was: all from Adam.

A small room beside the mosque in Medina. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is ill with a fever, and it isn't lifting. People come and go quietly. Aisha, his wife, is caring for him. And in these days, with little strength, the reports remember him busy with two things: giving things away, and one instruction he keeps coming back to. What does a person hold on to, at the very end, and what do they let go of? Today: the last days.
screen: `A SMALL ROOM IN MEDINA.` → `A FEVER THAT WON'T LIFT.` → `STILL BUSY, GIVING.`

segments.voice: Start with the coins. In a report in the Musnad of Ahmad, Aisha tells that during his illness he had a few gold coins at home, and he asked her to give them away. Then, in his fever, he asked again: what happened to the coins? She hadn't managed it yet, busy caring for him. He had them brought, and gave them away, and asked how it would be for him to meet his Lord with these still in his house. Then what he left. Sahih al-Bukhari records that when he died he left behind no dinar, no dirham, no slave, man or woman, nothing except his white mule, his weapons, and a piece of land he had given as charity. Whatever he had, he'd already let go of. And then what he held on to. Sunan Abu Dawud records his last instruction: the prayer, the prayer, and be mindful of God regarding those your right hands possess, the enslaved people and servants of a household. Of everything he could have said, he repeated that. Keep the prayer. Look after the people who are under your power. Coins given away the moment he remembered them. A house with nothing left to leave. And a last word that points away from things, toward the prayer and toward the people with the least power. Ali, who reports it, says these were his last words; Aisha remembers others. Tomorrow stays in that small room a little longer.

segments.voice: Picture a drawer, a shelf or a wallet, and find one thing you're keeping only because you haven't decided; choose it, and decide who it will go to. Then rest on the other half of his last words, the prayer and the people in your care: if you pray, let this be a moment to remember your next prayer; if not, bring to mind one person who depends on you.
The last days. In his final illness the Prophet gave away his last coins, left nothing behind, and asked, again and again, for the prayer to be kept. Today's word.
Your line: keep the prayer. Let go of the things; hold on to the prayer and the people. Until tomorrow.

797.title: Buried where he died
797.hook: he dies in Aisha's room and is buried there, now beneath the green dome in Medina
797.howItsDone: Muslims add a blessing of peace (salla Allahu alayhi wa sallam) whenever the Prophet is named, and visitors to the Prophet's Mosque in Medina stand before his resting place and greet him with peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last days, the coins given away, and the prayer asked for again and again. Your line was keep the prayer.

A curtain hangs where a door would be. Outside it, the companions have lined up for the dawn prayer, with Abu Bakr leading. Then, Anas reports in Bukhari, the curtain lifts. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, looks out at the rows praying, and smiles. The people nearly break their lines for joy. He signals to them to finish, and lets the curtain fall. It is one of the last things they see of him. The room behind it is Aisha's. Today, what happens in it, and why it is still there.
screen: `A ROOM BESIDE THE MOSQUE.` → `THE CURTAIN LIFTS.` → `HE SMILES AT THE ROWS.`

segments.voice: Aisha tells the next part herself. In her account in Bukhari, he died in her house, on the day that was hers, with his head resting against her. Her brother came in with a fresh tooth-stick, and she saw the Prophet's eyes follow it, so she softened it for him and he used it. Then the question of where to bury him. The companions did not agree. Abu Bakr settled it, according to a report in Tirmidhi, by remembering something he had heard the Prophet say: a prophet is buried in the place where he dies. They dug in the floor of the room, where the bed had been. That room is still there. Over time the mosque grew around it, and today it sits inside the Prophet's Mosque, under a green dome. Visitors stand before it and greet him: peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah. That greeting points to a verse. Surah al-Ahzab, verse fifty-six, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." This is salawat. Muslims say a short blessing after his name: salla Allahu alayhi wa sallam, God bless him and grant him peace. It's the little mark you see written after his name. Here the whole sirah we have walked since this block began comes to rest: Sumayyah, the boycott, Ta'if, the cave, Quba, the treaty, Mecca's open doors, the farewell at Arafah. Tomorrow the story turns to the people he left.

798.title: Who is a companion
798.hook: anyone who met the Prophet ﷺ as a believer and died a believer
798.howItsDone: Muslims add a phrase of respect after a companion's name, often radiya Allahu anhu, may God be pleased with him, and hadith scholars study the companions' lives in large biographical dictionaries.

segments.voice: Yesterday: buried where he died, and a greeting that goes everywhere. Your line was peace upon him.

Who counts? A merchant who spent years at his side, yes. But a traveler who came into Medina, met him once, accepted Islam, and rode home the same week? A small child brought to him for a blessing? A blind man who could never see his face? With the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, buried, the story of his life is told. A new block begins, and it belongs to the people around him. So first, a question hadith scholars had to answer: who is a companion?
screen: `A FRIEND OF YEARS?` → `A TRAVELER WHO MET HIM ONCE?` → `A BLIND MAN?`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is sahabi, one companion; the plural is sahabah. A close word, sahib, means a companion or comrade, and the Qur'an uses it for the Prophet himself, speaking to the people of Mecca. In Pickthall's translation of Surah an-Najm: "Your comrade erreth not, nor is deceived." Later scholars needed a precise meaning, because so much depends on it. A hadith travels down a chain of names, and the chain is meant to start with someone who was there. So a definition took shape, given by the hadith scholar Ibn Hajar among others: a companion is one who met the Prophet, believing in him, and died as a believer. Met, not saw, so that blind companions, like Ibn Umm Maktum, who called the prayer in Medina, are not left out. And the definition says nothing about how long. One meeting, as a believer, can be enough. So the circle is wide: famous names, and people we know only from one line in one report. How to weigh them is where Muslims differ. Sunni scholarship holds the companions as a whole to be trustworthy in what they passed on, and points to a hadith in Bukhari in which the Prophet says: don't revile my companions, for if one of you spent gold as much as the mountain of Uhud, it would not reach a small measure given by one of them, nor even half of it. Shia scholarship honors many companions deeply, and holds that each should be judged by what he or she did, not by the meeting alone. Both are asking the same question: who carried this to us, and how?

segments.voice: Let one face come, someone who was there for you in faith, or in whatever you hold most deeply: a grandmother at the stove, a teacher, a friend who answered a question late at night, someone you met only once. If you pray, make a quiet du'a for that person; if not, hold them in mind with thanks.
